lines: Imagine falling from the sky through a violent storm and waking up alone in a deadly jungle.
On 24 December 1971 a passenger plane is struck by lightning and breaks apart midair.
Seventeen year old Juliane Koepcke falls about 3000 meters while still strapped to her seat row.
She wakes up on the dark forest floor with a broken collarbone and a deep arm cut.
She also suffers from a painful eye injury and a severe concussion after the terrifying plunge.
Her biologist father previously taught her that following flowing water always leads back to people.
She finds a tiny creek and begins walking through the dense and dangerous Peruvian rainforest.
Days pass slowly as she follows the winding water toward a larger and safer river.
Up to 14 other passengers survive the initial crash but tragically die before any rescue arrives.
She spends 11 long days completely alone in the unforgiving jungle facing unimaginable odds.
After 9 days of difficult travel she finally discovers a remote lumberjack camp by the river.
She is found by local workers who provide medical help and bring her back to safety.
Juliane remains the only official survivor of LANSA Flight 508 against all odds and expectations.
Would you have the mental strength to survive 11 days alone in the dangerous rainforest?

lines: If you are lost in a dark forest at dusk, never hike toward a distant wooden cabin.
Cole is lost, and thick snow starts falling fast across the frozen woods around him now.
Night is coming in 20 minutes, but walking further will only make his danger much worse.
Searchers always start looking from your last known point, so Cole stays put near trees.
One. Cole stops moving immediately to follow the proven S.T.O.P. rule: Stop, Think, Observe, Plan.
He checks his cold surroundings and chooses a safe spot right next to a thick tree.
Two. Cole makes himself visible and audible in the open while staying near shelter.
He pulls out his bright orange jacket and crouches to remain clearly visible.
He blows 3 sharp whistle blasts into the cold air, the official signal for distress.
Three. Before total darkness arrives, Cole gets off the freezing cold ground without delay.
He gathers pine branches and dry leaves to build an insulating pad under his body.
He crouches tight against the wide tree trunk to shield himself from bitter wind.
Cole stays visible and waits quietly for the search and rescue team to locate him.
It was the perfect survival plan, but there was just one very serious problem.
The heavy snow is rapidly covering his bright jacket and hiding him from searchers.
part1.cliffhanger: Heavy snow is rapidly burying Cole's bright orange jacket and hiding his visual distress signal from rescuers.
